findings.where: The full-width blue band straight under the hero, 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' with its white Subscribe button (desktop at the fold; on phone it fills the second screen)
findings.fault: A second call to action, louder than the hero's own, sits right after the first screen. It is a saturated full-width field of house blue with a large centred display line and a white button, so after the headline and the face it is the heaviest thing on the page and outweighs the quiet 'Write to me directly' contact. It also offers something the page never shows: no briefings, no sign-up form, no sample. Subscribe goes only to #subscribe. The line also switches from Mark's 'I' to a marketer's 'Mark's', and its 'Get … / Subscribe' is the salesy register the brief rules out.
findings.who_objects: The bank official, who has just been told 'write to me directly' and now meets a newsletter pitch for a briefing service they cannot see or check. To them it reads as marketing rather than a personal advisor, and as a promise with nothing behind it. The founder would also object: the brief asks for one message and one quiet action, and says never to invent offers.

findings.where: Article specimen: the body paragraphs, the 'chapter topics' subhead, the numbered list and the closing paragraph (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: Mark's article is set centred, like an invitation, under a left-aligned title and byline. Every line starts at a different place, so the eye hunts for the next line through long legal paragraphs. In the numbered list the numbers stay at the left edge while their centred text drifts away from them, worst in item 2. This is the page that is meant to show his thinking in depth.
findings.who_objects: The official reading the article to judge whether Mark knows PPP law. Long centred prose is slow and tiring to read, and the detached list numbers make the structure hard to follow. Angélique would also object: every article she adds would inherit this.

findings.where: Hero, the lede under the headline (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The first screen never says that Mark works on law. The lede says he advises on infrastructure and PPPs, which any engineering or finance consultancy could say. Legislation, legal frameworks and drafting first appear far down, in the article specimen.
findings.who_objects: An official looking specifically for an independent legal advisor on a PPP law. In five seconds they cannot tell that this person drafts PPP legislation, and may move on. The brief also asks the page to reflect law, PPP and advice to governments.

findings.fault: Nothing on the first screen can be checked: no region or countries of his work, no named body that asked him, no recent talk or publication with its venue and date. Apart from the email address, the only evidence is a headline opinion and a photograph.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded official, who selects individuals against terms of reference by project kind and region. Before writing, they need to be sure this person has done such work for bodies like theirs.

findings.where: Hero top bar: 'Mark M. Moseley' and the MMM Infra mark
findings.fault: There is no navigation: no Articles, About/CV or Contact. The only link in the bar is the mark, which goes to #top. The brief's first screen calls for a nav, and the palette even assigns a colour to 'nav links' that do not exist.
findings.who_objects: The official who wants to read more, such as his CV, other papers or talks, before writing. They have no way to reach it and must scroll a homepage hoping it is there.

findings.where: Hero photograph: the keyed-out portrait on the slate ground (desktop; also the motion-sketch preview)
findings.fault: The brief asks for a full-bleed photo of Mark speaking. Instead his head and shoulders are cut from their backdrop and pasted onto flat slate, with a hard, slightly ragged mask round the hair. The figure ends abruptly at the bottom edge, and only a fragment of the microphone is left. It reads as a cut-out sticker, not a photograph in real light. (This is the candidate's keying and grading treatment, not the stand-in photo itself.)
findings.who_objects: A senior visitor used to institutional and law-firm sites, to whom a pasted cut-out looks cheap and slightly amateur. The founder would also object: the direction promised Mark at work in a real setting.

findings.where: The PDF card 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge' below the article
findings.fault: The card stacks a pale blue fill, a blue border, rounded corners and a wide soft drop shadow. Nothing else on this flat, square-cornered paper page has any of these, so it looks like a web-app widget dropped onto a document. It also shows a download icon and 'PDF', but the link goes to #article rather than to a file.
findings.who_objects: The reader, who expects a download from the icon and gets something else. The founder would also object to a gadgety element in a refined legal look; a hairline border with a wide soft shadow on one resting card breaks the house's surface rule.

findings.where: Section labels below the fold: 'PALETTE' (blue tracked capitals), 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' (small bold sans), 'Texture' (large italic serif)
findings.fault: The same level of label is set three different ways. 'PALETTE' is in tracked blue capitals, which breaks the page's own stated rules ('never tracked capitals', 'blue only where something can be clicked'). On a page where blue marks links, it makes a static label look like a link.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the tile as a system, for whom inconsistent labels undercut the specimen's claim to a coherent type system. A visitor may also try to click the blue label.
